document_title: Played Bethel's Yup'ik, the Model Answered Across the Sea
post_copy:
Meta's model card says "This model supports 4017 languages." "Supports" for Yup'ik means one label in 4,017.
The model named KYUK's Yup'ik clips Central Siberian Yupik 111 times and Yup'ik 110.

A four-label pilot trained on about 1,600 labeled clips across Yup'ik and Samoan lifted Yup'ik recall from 0.41 to 0.92.

Bethel's gold pin threads the slides past 111 pins on St. Lawrence Island, the label lists, KYUK's archive, the pilot, the speakers who label next and resolution 26-20.

In-house researchers wrote the pilot's labels. Community language fellows have begun labeling. Native-speaker annotators are planned.

AFN is set to take up 26-20 Saturday, October 24th. It seeks permanent and non-competitive federal language funding for Tribes, technology included. It never mentions AI.

What does a model builder owe the speakers who write the next labels?

#Yugtun #LanguageID #AFN2026

slides.headline: Played Bethel's Yup'ik, the model most often answered across the sea.
111 to 110.
slides.body: Played Yup'ik clips from KYUK's broadcasts, Meta's MMS-LID answered Central Siberian Yupik 111 times and Yup'ik 110. That language is spoken on St. Lawrence Island and in eastern Russia.

slides.headline: Three big open models list no Yupik at all.
slides.body: Only Meta's largest model lists Yup'ik, one label in 4,017. The authors say a label space that big makes out-of-the-box results poor for languages with little data.
labels: ONE TILE = ONE LANGUAGE A MODEL CAN NAME

slides.body: Central Siberian Yupik is a living language. One count puts about 1,000 speakers on St. Lawrence Island. The model's top miss was a near one.

slides.headline: The test audio came from Bethel's own station.
slides.body: KYUK airs about an hour of local news in Yup'ik a day. The researchers labeled 9 of its videos, 5.1 hours, through the American Archive of Public Broadcasting.

slides.headline: The labeled hours lifted recall to 0.92.
slides.body: Trained on labeled Yup'ik and Samoan clips, a small classifier on a frozen Whisper encoder lifted Yup'ik recall from 0.41 to 0.92. It chooses among four labels, not 4,017. The authors call it pilot-scale.

slides.headline: The next labels come from speakers.
slides.body: The pilot's labels were written by in-house researchers, not native speakers. The authors plan to hand that work to trained native-speaker annotators, and community language fellows have begun, the paper says.

slides.kicker: SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24TH · RESOLUTIONS SET FOR 10:15 A.M.
slides.headline: AFN is set to take up 26-20.
slides.body: From the Metlakatla and Ketchikan Indian Communities, it seeks permanent, non-competitive federal language funding for every eligible Tribe. Technology and archives are among its uses. It never mentions AI. Committee and board say do pass.

editor_notes_for_email: 0.92 is a PILOT result (C24, C29, C30). It comes from a four-label head trained on about 1,600 clips across the Yup'ik and Samoan sets, English segments included. It is not apples to apples with MMS-LID's 0.41 over 4,017 labels, and the esu and ess confusion is absent by construction. In replies, always pair the two numbers with 'four labels'.
26-20 never mentions AI (C58). The link from it to speech AI is the deck's own framing, not AFN's. It is still a draft and the delegates have not voted (C62), so never imply passage.
The about 1,000 speakers count for St. Lawrence Island Yupik (C51) is one undated estimate from the Alaska Native Languages site. Other counts run lower, and slide 04 says 'One count puts'.
Resolution 26-47 on Native radio funding is NOT in the deck or the sources. It names no stations, so never imply KYUK is among its 36.
